Rung half-muffled before a Festival of Commemoration in the church of Swindon's role in World War 1 - remembering especially Christ Church ringer, Private John H Odey of the Durham Light Infantry (killed in action, 8 June 1917), and Private William H Thomas of the Honourable Artillery Company (25 May 1917), in whose memory the second bell was given by his father.
During the Festival of Commemoration, tributes to John Odey and "Little Harry" Thomas were read, respectively, by a member of the band and a family member.
The tribute to John Odey was as follows:
"Like me, John Henry Odey was a bell-ringer.

Born in 1882 in Bath, where he learned to ring, John worked in the upholstery trade.  In May 1912, “J H O - upholsterer, mattress and blind maker”, placed a “situation wanted” notice in The Ringing World - then as now, the bell-ringers’ newspaper.

Later that year - with his wife, Rosie, and young children, Winifred and Stanley - John moved to Swindon to take up employment with Chandler Brothers.  The family resided just three hundred yards from here, at number three Stanley Street.

John joined the band of ringers at Christ Church.  Tower records show his exemplary attendance . . . until the 18th of September 1916 - when the register notes poignantly, “Left On His Majesty’s Service”.  He came back briefly to Swindon at Christmas.

In the New Year, Private Odey left for The Front with the Durham Light Infantry . . . he didn’t return.  On the 8th of June, John was killed during severe artillery bombardment of his battalion on the second day of the Battle of Messines.
A report of John’s death in The Ringing World recorded that “his services would be greatly missed by his fellow ringers, with whom his quiet, unassuming disposition made him very popular”.

John had been steeple-keeper at Christ Church, “where he carried out the duties entrusted to him in a painstaking and thorough manner”.  Like the present ones this evening, the bells he’d maintained were rung half-muffled “as a last token of respect to a departed comrade”.

Four years later, John’s widow received an official communication informing her of the exhumation of her late husband’s body.  Distressingly, a further letter from the War Office followed soon afterwards, apologising for a case of mistaken identity.
John Odey’s body was never recovered.  And at an auction in 1996, two of his medals were sold to an unknown buyer for just £20.

But his name lives on . . . amongst 54,000 others, all with no known grave, on the Menin Gate at Ypres . . . in Swindon, on the recently restored memorial over there by the south door, and the civic memorial in the Town Hall building . . . and on city, parish and bell-ringers’ memorials in Bath.

The hundredth anniversary of John’s death last year was commemorated with a full peal at Christ Church - three hours of continuous ringing - heard by three of his great-grandchildren, Angela, Martin and Terry.
And on this eve of the centenary of the Armistice, we honour John Odey tonight - along with so many others who made the ultimate sacrifice, a thousand of them from Swindon alone."

Today’s peal replicates a peal of Grandsire Triples rung here on 9th August 1913 which both William & George rang in, it being their first peal for both of them (it was in fact the first peal for all the band except the conductor). Rung near the centenary of the death of Private Arthur Townroe PO/505, Royal Marine Light Infantry, died of wounds 10th November 1918. Arthur enlisted at Mansfield (1914) for the Navy, but with an overspill of over 20,000 Royal Naval Volunteer Reserves, they were transferred into the Army which formed a Royal Naval Division. Arthur was drafted to serve with the 1st battalion ( Drake ) of the 1st Brigade. Initially posted to Gallipoli in April 1915, the battalion were deployed to France in May 1916. Private Townroe served the next two and half years on the Somme. On 31st October 1918, Arthur and the battalion were in billets at the village of Ambrines. On 9th November, the Drake battalion were eight miles south-east of Mons. At 11.15am, they moved forward to the village of Asquilles were they came under fire. During the advance Private Townroe was wounded and taken to the rear. Quote from a letter to his wife of six weeks from Private F Murphy " I am sorry to relate the last hours of your husband. When we picked him up we found there wasn't much chance of life left in him, the poor lad knew it himself...… I am please to say he was not in much pain, from the time he was hit, which would be around 12 midday, Sunday 10th November, he was conscious till 9pm. When I noticed a great change in him. He asked for a drink and told me to write to you. Then he asked to be moved and he never spoke again. We buried him with nine other men in a place called Asquillier……. Private Arthur Townroe is buried in Cement House Cemetery, XV11.B22 Ypres, Belgium.

In memory of Private John Rushton, Rishton, Lancashire. Died 04/11/1918 age 19. Lancashire Fusiliers 16th Bn. Service No.45341. Commemorated at Ors Communal Cemetery, France, Grave B 10. Born 2nd quarter 1899. One of seven children; five surviving at the 1911 census. Son of Nelson Rushton and Martha Alice Rushton (née Margerison) of 24 Commercial Street, Rishton, Lancashire. He was at school at the time of the 1911 census. He is remembered on the impressive war memorial at Rishton and on the Blackburn District War Memorial in Blackburn Cathedral ringing room. Born: Blackburn. Enlisted: Blackburn. Resided (1911 Census): 10 School Street, Rishton, Lancashire.

Note: In the row immediately behind John Rushton at Ors Communal Cemetery, in Grave A3, is buried Lieutenant Wilfred Edward Salter Owen MC, the well-known war poet who was also killed in action on 04/11/1918 while serving with the 5th Bn. Manchester Regiment.

Rung by the Potterhanworth, Coningsby & Old Bolingbroke ringers to celebrate Christmas prior to the Traditional Langton Candlelit Carol Service on the first Sunday after Chirstmas. The main body of Langton Church has no electric lighting so this was truly a proper candlelit carol service.
The bells at Langton are rung from the ground floor porch area by the main (only) Church door with the congregation walking through the centre of the ropes whilst we rang.
We also rang for a short time after the service as the congregation left the Church and made their way down to the village hall for seasonal refreshments.

It is fitting that these bells were rung this evening shortly before New Years Eve, as Tennyson was born just down the road at Somersby and would have heard these bells ringing out as a young boy, inspiring him to write ‘Ring Out Wild Bells’ part of ‘In Memoriam’ which he started in 1834 whilst at Somersby.
‘Ring out the old, ring in the new, Ring, happy bells, across the snow,
The year is going, let him go, Ring out the false, ring in the true.’

This quarter was being rung whilst the ancient medieval tradition in the City of ‘Crying Christmas’ took place which involves a procession down the High Street through the City led by the Lincoln Waites, finishing at the Guildhall, attended by the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, the City Sheriff, members of the City of Lincoln Civic Party and the Freemen of the City. Crying Christmas is a series of verses which were written for the City’s Civic Council in 1564.
Rung to mark the 504th anniversary of ‘Crying Christmas’ in the City of Lincoln.

Rung to the memory of Samuel Scattergood, rector at Blockley from 1681 to 1696. He was one of the leading lights of 17th century ringing and contributed several new methods to the first known book on ringing, Fabian Stedman’s Campanalogia, published in 1677. The 5th of the present ring was cast during his incumbency. Samuel joined the College Youths in 1672 and was master in 1685. He died in 1696 and was buried on 10th December under the chancel in this church. The band consists of 5 ringers who helped with the restoration and augmentation project plus five past and present master of the Society.

Rung half-muffled on the centenary of the death of Archibald Bertie Alexander.  Archibald Alexander was born on 4 February 1899 and lived with his parents and brother in Buxhall, where his occupation was recorded as Carter.  He enlisted at Bury St Edmunds on 4 January 1917, a month before his 18th birthday, and was originally sent to serve as a Private in the 2/1st Herts. Yeomanry but was soon transferred to the Stafford Cyclists Regiment. On 18 August 1918 he landed in France and joined the 1st North Staffordshire Regiment. Just a few days before the Armistice his battalion was in action a few miles south east of Valenciennes.  In the early hours of 4 December he was admitted to No.24 General Hospital where he told staff that he had been gassed a month before.  He died of nephritis later that day.  Private Archibald Bertie Alexander, aged 19 years, is buried in Etaples Military Cemetery, France.

Rung on the back bells on the centenary of the Clun Armistice 'Peace Peal' that marked the successful termination of the war by Great Britain and her Allies. The 'Peace Peal' was also the first peal on the eight bells that were rung today - the method and composition rung today were the same as those rung 100 years ago. It is exactly 350 years since the recast ring of five bells and the restored tower were opened after having being destroyed by fire during the Civil War. First peal: 8; First peal on eight: 1.

In memory of Private William Austin Hamer, Glasbury. Died 04/12/1918 age 19. South Wales Borderers 1st Bn. Service No.46813. Buried at Charmes Military Cemetery, Essegney, France, Grave I G 7. Born first quarter of 1899 and baptised 05/02/1899 at Builth Wells. One of eight children, seven surviving at the 1911 census. Son of John Hamer and Sarah Hamer (née Lewis) of Pontneddfechan, Glamorgan. He was at school at the time of the 1911 census when he lived in Clarence Cottage, Velindre and later worked as a coal miner at the Empire Colliery, Glynneath.  Enlisted in Neath.  He had been captured by the Germans on 18/04/1918 and was one of the first prisoners of war to be returned to the British authorities in France after the armistice. His mother was informed that he was malnourished and was “nothing but bones”. He contracted pneumonia on 26/11/1918 and later died at No.42 Stationary Hospital. A memorial peal of Doubles with three covering tenors was rung at this church on 04/01/1920 for Private Hamer and two other fallen Glasbury servicemen ringers.

Rung to commemorate Sapper Edward (Ned) Gent, Whittle-le-Woods, Lancashire. Died 01/12/1918 age 34. Royal Engineers 13th Anti-Aircraft Searchlight Sect. Service No.466351. Commemorated at Whittle-Le-Woods (St. John) Churchyard, England, Grave in south-west part. Born 11/11/1884. One of seven children; six surviving at the 1911 census. Son of John Gent of Glencoe House, Whittle-le-Woods and the late and Mary Gent (née Garstang, died 1915). Husband of Annie Gent (née Knowles) whom he married on 14/04/1909 at St John’s Whittle-le-Woods, of Lytham View, Whittle-le-Woods. Father of Bessie Gent (born 03/11/1914) He rang his first peal, ringing the tenor and conducting Plain Bob Major at Whittle-le-Woods on 01/02/1913. He rang in and conducted a peal of Plain Bob Major at Chorley (RC) Church on 27/09/1913, the footnote to the peal reported that the “go of them is anything but good”. He rang a peal at Chorley Parish Church, also Plain Bob Major, on 27/09/1913. He worked as a blacksmith for Mr B. Harrison in Chorley before enlisting. On Armistice day, 11/11/1918, his 34th birthday, he wrote to his father and sisters “did ever anyone have a more blessed birthday gift … no more dodging bombs and shrapnel, and machine gun fire”. He had written to his family describing life in the trenches and had ‘seen some pitiful sights’ in Verdun, Lens, Bethune, La Bassée, Vimy and Lille. After three years of active service in France he was given leave of a few days, after walking from Wigan railway station to Chorley in cold, wet and windy November weather he succumbed to influenza and pneumonia and died within days of reaching home. A memorial peal of Kent TB Major was rung to his memory on 21/04/1923 at Whittle-le-Woods, which was conducted by William Lancaster. Born: Chorley. Enlisted: Unknown. Resided (1911 Census): Paradise Row, Whittle-le-Woods.
